title: Jacob shows favoritism again in old age — Genesis 48
paragraphs: Jacob shows favoritism again in old age — Genesis 48
He was old. Weak-eyed. Near death.
And still, Jacob reached for one son over another.

Genesis 48 is uncomfortable because it feels familiar. The same man who grew up in a house poisoned by favoritism now seems to repeat the pattern in old age. He takes Joseph’s sons, Manasseh the firstborn and Ephraim the younger, then deliberately crosses his hands and gives the greater blessing to the younger.

That scene stings because sin has a way of aging with us when it is not fully surrendered to God. Wounds we survived can become wounds we pass on. Patterns we hated can become patterns we repeat. Jacob knew what favoritism cost a family. He had lived inside its smoke.

Genesis 48 is not only about a broken old man. It is also about a sovereign God. Some scholars interpret Jacob’s crossed hands as lingering favoritism. Others see it primarily as prophetic discernment under God’s guidance, because Jacob says he knows what he is doing and the blessing follows God’s surprising pattern of lifting the younger over the older. The text gives us both tension and mystery.
And that is where grace walks in.

Because even when human hands are crossed, God’s purposes are not confused. Even when fathers fail, God does not fail. Even when family lines are bent by weakness, the covenant mercy of God keeps moving forward.
That is the Gospel shadow in Genesis.

Not perfect men.
Not perfect fathers.
Not perfect homes.

Jesus stepped into a world wrecked by envy, rivalry, birthright battles, and generational pain. And instead of adding to the curse, He carried it. At the cross, the true Firstborn took our place so the undeserving could receive blessing. In Christ, the rejected are brought near. In Christ, the cycles can break. In Christ, grace is stronger than inheritance.

So read Genesis 48 with open eyes:
old age does not automatically mean holiness,
family pain does not disappear by itself,
and God’s mercy is still writing a better ending than our failures deserve.

Maybe you came from a house marked by comparison.
Maybe you were the overlooked one.
Maybe you were the favored one and it damaged you too.

Repent where you have repeated what once wounded you.
Receive where you have carried what was never yours to keep.
And trust the God who can straighten what generations have crossed.
